title: How I Trained My Memory, and What It Taught Me About Learning
author: fivetwelvethirteen
summary: The author uses a memory-palace project (PAO system for 100 random digits in five minutes) as a laboratory for learning itself, laying bare principles difficult to see in ordinary teaching. Component skills are what you practise; the headline skill is emergent. Small chunks beat large ones, vivid connections are what make retrieval possible, varied practice beats repetitive drill, and effortful retrieval is what produces durable memory. Transfer is narrower than it feels: getting better at digits does not automatically help with names. The take-home is not a new trick but a cleaner picture of what happens when a pupil gets better at anything hard, and a rebuttal to the idea that memory does not matter in the age of AI. Memory training builds the mental scaffolding that makes thought possible, and the gains are indistinguishable from subject consolidation in school.
points: The headline skill you want is emergent from component skills you practise separately; you do not practise the final goal, you practise its parts and then integrate.
Effortful retrieval is what produces durable memory; the moment a recall feels hard is the moment the learning is working, not failing.
Transfer is narrower than intuition suggests; getting better at one thing does not automatically help with similar tasks unless transfer is specifically built on purpose.
quotes: I spent several months training myself to memorise 100 random digits in five minutes. It worked. I can now do it, most days. But the interesting thing is not the result. The interesting thing is what the training revealed about how learning works.

The headline skill — memorise 100 digits in 5 minutes — is emergent. It’s made up of component skills you practise separately, the way a pianist practises scales, chord shifts, and sight-reading before ever playing a piece.
Small chunks beat large ones. Every time I tried to process more than a few digits at a time, my accuracy collapsed. Every time I stuck to the two-digit chunk the PAO system uses, I was fine.
The connection is everything. The vivid, often absurd story linking one image to the next is what makes retrieval possible at speed. A bland connection is a broken connection.
Varied practice beat repetitive practice. The days I mixed in different digit sequences, different starting points, different distractions, I got better faster than the days I drilled the same thing.

Effortful retrieval is where the durable learning lives. The moment a recall felt easy, I was usually about to get it wrong the next time. The moment it felt hard, I was usually about to strengthen it.

Distraction has a measurable cost. I could see it in my own timings, reliably, before I could feel it subjectively. Five seconds of checking a phone cost me ten seconds of recall speed on the next attempt.

Transfer is narrower than it feels. Getting better at memorising digits did not make me better at remembering names, or facts in a meeting. Transfer is a skill you have to build on purpose; it does not come free with practice.” Archived from fivetwelvethirteen on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
